On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya was the one in command and Sitaram was the subordinate guard, even being bound by Udayaditya’s order. By the night of Udayaditya’s own escape from prison, the roles reverse: Sitaram becomes the active rescuer and guide, coming to free Udayaditya from prison and leading him out, while Basanta Ray is the one being hurried along by Sitaram.

Pratapaditya’s first plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray when he stayed at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; that plan failed. The method that finally succeeded was Pratap’s order to Muktiyar Khan to carry out the death sentence, and Abdul then killed Basanta Ray with a drawn sword.
In the inner quarters, disguised as a woman, and in the palace room, disguised as a jester.
A covert poisoning arranged by Mangala (Rukmini) — with the Mahishi secretly fetching the poison/medicine — caused Surma to take poison and die, rather than a simple exile to her father’s house.
It leads to a tragic outcome: Ramchandra Ray, enraged by Vibha’s refusal, takes another wife, and Vibha is left behind in her own kingdom with no place in her husband’s home.

Udayaditya’s signet ring was used as the seal on a forged petition that falsely appeared to be the Yubaraj’s complaint against Pratapaditya; Bhagavat presented that petition to Pratapaditya as if it were an authentic document sent by Udayaditya, and Pratapaditya, believing it, ordered Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Because Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape made Pratapaditya pay special attention to Udayaditya; when he then learned that Udayaditya had secretly arranged stipends for the dismissed guards, he interpreted it as Udayaditya’s defiance and issued the decree sending Surma away.

The song carries a deep emotional meaning of loneliness, loss, and emptiness: it is Basanta Ray’s lament that he is left alone while what once belonged to him has gone away, and he can no longer find the joy or companionship he once had. Basanta Ray sings it in two contrasting contexts: first, in Raigarh, when he is alone and sings it to himself as a spontaneous expression of his own sorrow and fading joy; second, in Jessore, when he sees the once-happy household now empty and silent, and he sings it while holding Vibha’s hand as a sorrowful acknowledgment that the family’s joy has vanished.

Because Rukmini failed to stop Udayaditya’s midnight escape, Udayaditya reached Raigarh, and Pratapaditya then ordered Muktiyar Khan to carry out the death sentence for Basanta Ray, who was killed when that order was executed.

Pratapaditya initially gave Ramchandra a minimal, almost dismissive reception, but later Ramchandra, in his own court, treats Pratapaditya as a superior figure and speaks of him with deference rather than with the same disrespect.

She re-enters as Mangala (the same Rukmini from Raigarh), living on the outskirts of Jessore and using palace connections to learn of Surma’s situation; she then prepares a poison and, with the Rajmahishi’s secret help, causes Surma’s death, after which she later appears in Udayaditya’s bedchamber and brings further tragedy by claiming his love and stirring his grief.

Udayaditya’s early lament about being the crown prince—his belief that he is unfit to rule and that his father has lost faith in him—eventually culminates in a formal renunciation of the throne. After being brought before Pratapaditya, he states that he is not worthy of the kingdom and asks to be released from the throne. Then, in front of Ma-Kali, he takes an oath that he will never accept any part of Jessore’s kingdom, will not sit on the throne, and will not even touch the royal scepter, with Samaraditya named as the heir.

Nayanchand intercepted Ramchandra Ray’s letter and gave it to the Mahishi; the Mahishi then misrepresented it to Vibha as a letter from Ramchandra requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip, and she announced this in the household.

Pratapaditya blocked the canal with large sal-wood logs, but Ramchandra Ray’s boat was pulled up and over the obstruction by Rammohan and his followers, allowing the midnight escape to succeed; the guards then failed to catch up because their boat was delayed and they were too late.

Basanta Ray’s beloved sitar becomes a symbol of his despair: he leaves it behind when he departs, later says its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned, and he sings only a mournful song about being “left behind,” showing that his attachment to the sitar mirrors his growing grief over Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for boldly intervening to protect the oppressed and oppose injustice; after Surma’s death, he becomes fearful and hesitant, unable to help the subjects and even avoiding intervention out of fear of Pratapaditya.
He undoes it by setting the prison on fire and helping Udayaditya escape from it, thereby reversing the harm caused by the forged petition.

On the first desperate occasion, Rammohan made a long rope from thick sheets, tied it to a roof-side pillar, climbed down with Ramchandra on his back, and lowered him into the boat; on the second, he lifted the unconscious Vibha from the palace and placed her in a palanquin to take her out.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed in a heavily ornate, royal-style presentation—thick gold bangles, a large diamond bracelet, a large nose ring, and a heavily styled coiffure imposed by the Mahishi. In Chandradwip, she is instead dressed as a plain common woman (like a beggar-woman), without the elaborate adornments or royal presentation, and goes to seek Ramchandra Ray in that humble, unadorned form.

In Udayaditya’s bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window symbolizes longing and hope—he keeps expecting Surma to appear there, and it becomes a place of grief and imagined reunion. In the prison cell, the window changes into a symbol of freedom and liberation: through it he sees a small patch of sky and the birds, which makes him believe that one day he too will be released, while the bed in the room represents the true prison.

Sitaram first comes to Rukmini as a man in need of money, and she responds with flirtatious, affectionate language while lending him cash. He, in turn, becomes increasingly infatuated and starts making witty, romantic advances, even calling her “Subhadra” and “Priyatame,” while she plays along and laughs. As his financial desperation grows, he keeps visiting her and eventually enters into secret schemes with her. When Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram’s anger and obsession turn into threats against Rukmini’s house and the Yubaraj’s fate. In response, Rukmini becomes furious and, after the prison fire and the rumor of Udayaditya’s death, she turns into a dangerous, vengeful figure—warning that she will “lay [Sitaram] and the Yubaraj in the oven” and threatening him with a blade. In other words, what begins as a flirtatious financial arrangement becomes a violent, life-threatening confrontation, with Sitaram’s obsession and Rukmini’s rage pushing the relationship into deadly territory.

Sitaram starts by using the guardhouse fire as a distraction—he and his men create chaos, misdirect the guards, and make the fire seem like a real emergency so no one pays close attention to Udayaditya’s prison. Once the fire spreads, he has his men set Udayaditya’s prison cell ablaze, throw bones, a skull, and the Yubaraj’s sword into it, and then spread the story that the Yubaraj died in the fire. At the same time, he secretly escorts Udayaditya out, destroys or keeps letters to cover the escape, and leaves the palace servants to blame one another while he flees Jessore with his family.
Ramchandra Ray later treats Udayaditya’s conduct in his court as a self-serving, sister-centered act and turns it into a subject of ridicule rather than gratitude.

By forging a petition in Udayaditya’s name and presenting it to Pratapaditya as if it were headed for the Emperor of Delhi, Bhagavat turned the Emperor’s political power into the pretext for action; Pratapaditya then used that “complaint” as justification to imprison his son.

In the Jessore palace, Vibha’s hair was a visible sign of Surma’s presence: Surma used to braid it to her liking, and when Surma was there, Vibha’s hair was styled and cared for. After Surma’s tragic absence, Vibha’s hair remains unbraided and she sits waiting for Surma to come, showing that Surma is no longer present.
